claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is a homogeneous, disordered BCC solid solution after holding at 900 °C for 1 h.
Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between Al-driven ordering enthalpy and the configurational entropy of disordered BCC.
Al-driven ordering enthalpy favors formation of a B2 phase.
Configurational entropy stabilizes disordered BCC at high temperature.
Diffusive kinetics of Al partitioning determine the observable phase state during cooling.
Slow cooling permits Al diffusion and lowers the alloy's enthalpy through formation of ordered B2 regions.
Rapid water quenching freezes in the high-temperature, disordered BCC state.
Cooling rate changes the extent of Al–Cr ordering and B2 nanocluster formation within the BCC matrix.
A water-quenched sample will remain predominantly disordered BCC and show no B2 superlattice peaks in XRD.
A water-quenched sample will have lower hardness than a slowly cooled sample.
Furnace cooling at 10 °C/min will produce B2 ordering detectable through distinct superlattice XRD peaks.
Furnace cooling at 10 °C/min will increase hardness by approximately 10–20% relative to water quenching.
The proposed comparison holds composition, 900 °C hold time, atmosphere, sample mass, and sample geometry constant while varying cooling rate.
The water-quenched specimen is the baseline for comparison with the specimen furnace-cooled at 10 °C/min.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, cooling rates above 100 °C/s for quenching and below 10 °C/min for furnace cooling, and holds no longer than 1 h at 900 °C.

contradictions.description: The slow-cooling experiment is specified at exactly 10 °C/min, whereas the stated boundary requires furnace-cooling rates below 10 °C/min, so the proposed test lies outside the strict stated boundary.
